He'd tell you to stop working on the price and work on the other side of the deal. To him, value is the dream outcome times how likely the buyer thinks they are to get it, divided by how long it takes and how much effort it costs [1]. A price cut changes none of those four things. So he'd ask: can you make the result come faster, make it feel more certain, and make it easier to get? If not enough people say yes, his answer is always to make the offer better. He calls that the highest-leverage thing in a business [2].

**Speed first.** He ranks a short wait above a bigger result ("latency beats magnitude") and says wealthier buyers are sold more on time saved than money saved [3]. The simplest move he names is to take your current delivery time and cut it in half [4]. If you already have more demand than you can handle, charge for speed directly. One example is a 20% priority fee to jump the queue, refunded if you miss the deadline. As he puts it, "speed's all margin" [5].

**Then likelihood and ease.** Buyers believe they'll get the result when they see you as competent and clearly trying to help them. One-on-one delivery and a track record raise that belief a lot [6]. You can also take on their risk: sell a guarantee or a warranty, or absorb delays and difficulty, and charge a premium for doing so [7]. For ease, go through your own customer experience, note every action the customer has to take, and delete as many as you can [8].

**Build the premium version.** Ask what you'd include if you charged 10x. Most of those ideas don't cost much [9]. Assume this buyer is a different, wealthier person than your current one, and sell to whoever values the result most [10]. He'd also push back on the instinct behind your question: raising the price can *add* value, because it makes buyers more confident you'll deliver. If you close more than 80% of sales, you're probably underpriced [11]. The one case where he'd lower anything is when your ideal customers, not just anyone, keep saying price is the problem. Then he'd add a cheaper tier rather than discount the main offer [12].

What would change his answer: if your offer already converts well, he'd leave it alone and work on your marketing instead.

Yes, he'd tell you to admit them, and to put them right at the front. He calls damaging admissions possibly his favorite ad tactic and says "nothing more powerful" exists in his experience [1]. His reasoning is that your prospect is already thinking about your flaws. If you say them first, you take the objection away and earn trust. "What you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise," and he would "always sacrifice promise to gain trust" [2]. Anyone can claim the best product, so that claim doesn't stand out. What stands out is that "what people won't say is the truth" [4].

**How to word it.** Use one structure: a true thing that hurts you, then "but," then the claim you want believed. Whatever comes after "but" is what the reader remembers, so the order matters:

- "These markers smell like crap, but they write four times longer than other markers and don't dry out." That's more believable than stating the benefit alone [3].
- "Our websites are ugly as hell but they convert." "Our systems are incredibly boring but they work." [3]
- If you flip the order ("our systems work but they're boring"), the reader takes away "boring." **The admission always goes first and the selling point goes last.** [3]
- He gives more points for humor. His gym example: "our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking our AC is kind of on and off i don't have the best equipment but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's" [4]. You end up believing the classes are fun, which you wouldn't if the ad just said "we have the most fun sessions."

**How to find your admissions.** Write down every flaw, every complaint customers make and everything you know you could do better. Then claim them [3]. Pick admissions that are true, that a prospect would actually believe, and that make your main claim easier to believe. For example, cheap and plain can make "it works" more credible, and small or slow can make "personal" more credible.

He uses the same move in sales. For an offer that sounds too good to be true, he opens with "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad" and lists what's wrong with it [5]. For a travel-points business, that meant "you can have what you want, just not when you want." People who can't live with that trade-off drop out on their own, so the ones left "can self-qualify" [6]. Your ad can work the same way. If you name the person a weakness rules out, you're also calling out who the ad is *not* for, and he rates that as even stronger than saying who it is for [7].

What would change his answer: nothing in what he's said. He presents this as always applying, not as something that depends on the situation. The only condition is that the flaw has to be true, because the whole tactic works by being honest.

**Write it at a third-grade reading level, same as for anyone else.** Hormozi wouldn't make an exception for educated business owners. His rule is about attention, not intelligence. Then run every ad through a free reading-level checker and keep editing until it scores third grade. He says he does that with every ad he writes [6].

His reasoning is that most copy fails because the reader has to pause to understand it, and the moment they pause, they stop. Reading the copy "takes more horsepower than they're willing to dedicate to it" [1]. A business owner with a degree is still scrolling fast, still distracted and still doesn't care about you yet. So he tells you to assume every prospect is "in a rush," doesn't care, reads below a third-grade level and is distracted [1]. Even a reader who can easily handle ninth-grade prose won't spend the effort on an ad. "You're not writing a college paper," you're writing an ad with milliseconds to catch someone [2]. If you write at ninth grade, he says you "automatically disqualify two-thirds" of readers, and the bestselling books in America are written simply on purpose [3]. His audience is business owners too, and he still writes his own ads this way.

In practice that means short sentences, small words, big promises and big proof, and "few adverbs and better verbs" [4]. When fewer words and simpler words conflict, pick the simpler words: "simplicity trumps concision" [4]. Speak to your educated audience through what you say, not through bigger words. Call out exactly who the ad is for, and who it isn't for, and write to that one person [5]. Good copy should make the words "fade into the background" so the reader only sees the idea [2].

He never gave a case where higher-level writing converts better. A side-by-side test where the plainer version lost would be the only thing that might change his mind, and he'd expect the plain version to win.

He has described almost exactly your situation. When he explains his "one thing" question (what one thing, if it were true 12 months from now, would change everything?), his example is an HVAC company short on technicians. The owner starts a recruiting search, a referral network or internships, and "one month in" the new hires still haven't come [1][2]. His answer is that a big fix can take time, and you sometimes "have to sit with the pain of an unbuilt bridge without building a second bridge" [1]. He admits he does what you're thinking of doing. He starts a big solution, gets impatient after about 30 days, and wants to try another way. He calls that a mistake, because working on it two or three ways "ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" [3]. He'd rather make one sure bet with the most leverage than many small bets, which he calls "death by a thousand paper cuts" [3].

So put your effort into making the current push work better, not into adding new ones. He always improves the existing channel before he'll add a new one [5]. For recruiting, he says to treat the people you want to hire as your new customer, and to market to them the way you market to buyers [4]. In practice, the job this month is to work on that push's offer to technicians, its ads and its follow-up. Starting a parallel program would take people and money away from it.

What would change his answer: this only holds if the push you started is the right bet, meaning the one approach you believe will work if you give it time. If you've lost confidence in the approach itself, you'd replace it with a better single bet, not run three at once. That part is inferred from his rule; he didn't say it. Also, the small daily improvements to lead flow, close rate and margin don't count against the one thing, so keep doing those.

Hormozi would tell you that 20% monthly churn is average for a paid online community, under 10% is what the best ones hit, and you should worry once more than 30% leave each month. Above that line, retention is your highest-ROI fix and comes before anything else, including getting more members [1]. Before you judge your number, split it by how long members have been in. Most of the churn is new people.

**The benchmarks.** These are Skool platform averages, which he says apply to online and remote consumer services, not things like insurance or alarm systems [1]:

| Monthly churn | Retention | Where you stand |
|---|---|---|
| under 10% | over 90% | best groups |
| about 20% | about 80% | platform average |
| 30% or more | 70% or less | work on retention before anything else |

He stresses how much those few points matter. Going from 20% to 10% churn isn't a 10% improvement. It doubles how long the average member stays, so it doubles their lifetime value [2].

**When to worry.** His "biggest rule" is that churn falls steeply with tenure [3]:
- **Months 1–3:** 20% or more churn is normal.
- **After day 90:** it drops to about 10% or less.
- **By month 6:** it falls to around 2%.

So a community under 90 days old will always show inflated churn, because nobody has reached the low-churn months yet. A community under six months old is inflated too, just less so. He says outright not to "overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks." The exception is when basically everyone is leaving [4]. The real warning sign is members who have been in for months still leaving at high rates.

**What to do about it.** He'd have you stop asking "how do I push the average down?" and ask "how do I get people past day 90 and month six?" [5]
- **First month:** onboarding, setting expectations, selling the right promise, and showing up daily.
- **Day 90:** members need a real outcome or a change in behavior.
- **Month 6:** members need connections with other people in the community [6].

Track joins against cancels every month and label yourself growing, flat or declining [7]. DM everyone who cancels, tag their reason, and every 20 or so cancels fix the top one or two reasons [8]. Overwhelm is the biggest cause of churn after price [9].

A different benchmark set could change his answer. He says these numbers don't fit things like insurance premiums or alarm systems [1]. Also keep in mind that all of this comes from Skool's data, and Skool is a platform he promotes and talks about as "us."

Take the percentage of revenue. Hormozi has addressed this exact choice, and he'd say a rev share is "way better" than a profit share [2].

His reasoning is that profit is a number the client controls. They decide what to spend, so they "can play around their profit" and overspend, and your cut shrinks even when your work is paying off. Revenue is harder to adjust: "top line's top line" [2][3]. His general rule for any deal is that you want to be paid "no matter what" and paid "first", off the top. That's why he values royalties and licensing [4]. He even names your situation: he lists "consulting agreements that are percentage of profit or revenue" as one of the outcome-based ways to get paid, and revenue is the one higher up his ladder [1].

He adds one condition. Being paid on outcomes means you carry some of the risk, and he says you can only take that on "when you're good" [5]. His view is that you're paid in proportion to the risk you take [6]. So if you're confident you can move the client's top line, take the rev share and expect it to beat a fee. If you aren't, the problem is your offer, not which percentage you pick. A related idea, which he applied to employees rather than consultants: he suggests taking a lower base in exchange for more upside if things go well. A small retainer plus a revenue share would be one way to apply that to you.

**What would change his answer:** he never compared a small revenue percentage with a much larger profit percentage. Before you accept, run both offers on the client's real numbers. Also, his worry is that the client spends money you have no say over. If your contract gives you real control over their costs, the gap between the two options gets smaller. That second point is my inference, not something he said.

Bootstrap. For a first business, Hormozi says to fund it from your own savings and cash flow, with no outside investors, and grow by reinvesting profits [1]. His main reason is that you need to "pay off ignorance debt" first. You don't yet know what you're doing, and the worst outcome is losing your friends' and family's money while you learn [2]. He'd also tell you not to raise much from anyone on your first try, including VCs [3].

He's open about what it costs. Bootstrapping is slow, because you're building the business that makes the money and the money to grow it at the same time [4]. It also leaves you with other kinds of debt. You can't afford star hires or top tools, so you pile up management, leadership and technical debt, which he says is often harder to pay off than money [5]. In return you keep control and equity [6]. Your costs stay low, so you can survive a lot longer, though having little capital limits how big you can start [7]. So pick something cheap to start that people already pay for: a service, an agency, a local business, education or e-commerce. Don't bet on an untested idea [8]. Cut your personal costs first so you can afford the risk [9].

He thinks raising money fits one specific case. That's a big idea that can't become profitable without other people's money: large upfront costs, years of losses, or a winner-takes-all market [10]. Competitors look down on repairs, and he likes to build around work others ignore and then set it up to earn good gross profit [4]. Volume gives you stability. - **A cheap maintenance membership:** about $15–20 a month, with $2 credited toward future repairs for every $1 paid. Its real value is the yearly visit, which is another chance to sell [8].

**This isn't Hormozi's story. It's Steven Bartlett's.** He told it while interviewing Hormozi on *The Diary of a CEO* (April 2023). Hormozi's part was the reply, where he turned it into his own rule: do the same work for the people who value it most.

**Bartlett's story.** His first company went public on a stock exchange in Europe. Later they considered another IPO and met about 20 investment banks on a roadshow. The banks told him the exact same business would be worth four times more on the NASDAQ, so his net worth would quadruple just by changing exchanges [1]. Years later he applied that idea to his own skills in social media, marketing and storytelling. He asked where those skills were scarcest, most in demand and best paid. His answer was companies about to IPO, because a good story can move a valuation by hundreds of millions. The first company he worked with listed at about $3 billion. His equity for 9–12 months of what was "basically freelance" work was worth roughly $7–8 million on IPO day [2]. That's why he started Flight Story, which began in the IPO market [2].

**What Hormozi took from it.** He agreed and put numbers on it with conversion-rate work. Raise a $1M e-commerce store's conversion by 20% and you've created $200K of value; take 10% and you earn $20K. Do the same work for a $100M business and you've created $20M and earn $2M. That's 100x the pay for the same work [3]. His summary was "solve rich people problems they pay better," or in other words, "find the people who value what you have the most" [3]. He added a parable about a beat-up car. A dealer offers $1,000 for it and a scrapyard offers $500, but an antique dealer recognizes it as a rare historic car worth $100,000 [4]. Later he put Bartlett's NASDAQ example into his own leverage ladder. Capital goes from friends and family, to institutional money, to public money, and each step has far more capital behind it [5].

So the answer he'd give you: before you work harder, find the market that values your skill the most.

Sellers outside the EU owe it from the first sale. EU-based sellers get a combined €10,000 threshold for cross-border sales. **Know where the risk sits.** He says the question behind every deal is "who's got the risk", and that you get paid in proportion to the risk you carry [3]. When the payout is deferred, you are still betting on the business, just without control of it. If you choose to carry that risk, he'd want you paid for it. He'd also want it to be a risk you understand better than the market does. He calls that a mispriced bet [4].

**Keep the buyout debt small and pay it off fast.** ESOPs are usually funded with debt the company takes on. On business debt he says he leans "very close to the Ramsey side", because "risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due" [5]. A company loaded with debt to buy you out can miss payments in a bad year, and you'd be one of the people waiting to be paid.

**Keep the deal simple.** He calls complexity "the child of lazy thinking" [6]. Use the plainest structure that works, and don't stack earn-outs and side deals on top of it.

**Bottom line:** In his framing, an employee buyout is a "when X happens, you pay me" deal: you get paid when the business performs. He'd push you to move it toward "you pay me first, no matter what." What would change this answer: if a buyer offers you more cash up front, his rules favor that buyer. That applies even if it's private equity, which is how he sold two-thirds of his own companies for $46.2M [7].

The details of an ESOP (a trustee, an independent valuation, tax deferral when you sell, how the bank loan and your seller note are ranked) are not covered anywhere in his material. Get an ESOP attorney and a valuation firm for those.
